**Measured, not published.** No flight manual for this aeroplane is public, so there is no handbook stall speed to hold the model to. This is what the model itself does, flown by the same deceleration the published stall speeds are measured by, on 2026-09-23. What it asserts is that the model still does what it did, not that the aeroplane does it. Measured from entry speeds of 160, 200 and 240 knots it varies by 1.21 of a knot, so the number is the model's and not the entry's.

**Measured, not published.** No flight manual for this aeroplane is public, so there is no handbook rate of climb and no handbook climbing speed. Both are the model's own, taken on 2026-09-23. The curve is still flat here, so the speed is not what the ninety-five per cent test picked but the floor under it: **1.3 times the measured stall speed of 151.1 knots**, the lowest speed at which it is sensible to climb. A fighter has so much thrust to spare that it climbs within a few per cent of its best rate over hundreds of knots, and taking the peak would have taught a climb at 522 knots.
